Decisions

I find it really hard to make decisions

Having many options can paralyse you. Settling for "good enough" usually brings more satisfaction.

Agonising for weeks over which phone to buy, which flat to rent or which degree to study. Comparing, reading reviews and, when you finally choose, thinking that maybe the other option was better.

Maximisers and satisficers

The psychologist Barry Schwartz and colleagues proposed in 2002 distinguishing between two styles. Maximisers always look for the best possible option and compare every alternative. Satisficers set some criteria and choose the first option that meets them, without worrying whether something slightly better existed.

The surprising thing is that maximisers, although they sometimes get objectively slightly better results, feel less satisfied with their choices, regret more and are more prone to sadness. Looking for the best has a cost.

Too many options

The more alternatives there are, the harder it is to decide and the easier it is to regret, because there is always a rejected option that might have been better. Many decisions are also tiring.

The trap of being able to change your mind

We tend to prefer reversible decisions, such as being able to return a purchase. Daniel Gilbert and Jane Ebert found that people who could change their choice ended up less satisfied than those who could not. When a decision is final, the mind looks for its advantages and settles; when it remains open, we keep comparing. Sometimes committing to an option is what lets you enjoy it.

Does willpower run out?

It has been said that making many decisions in a row "uses up" the ability to decide well, so-called decision fatigue. A famous study of Israeli judges seemed to show that they granted fewer paroles before the lunch break, but other researchers pointed out that the order of cases was not random. In addition, a large study across 23 laboratories failed to reproduce the "ego depletion" effect. What does seem useful is to make important decisions when rested rather than at the end of the day.

What usually helps

  • Decide in advance what is "good enough" and choose the first option that meets it.
  • Limit the options: compare three, not thirty.
  • Set a deadline for deciding.
  • Separate important decisions from unimportant ones: not all deserve the same effort.
  • Remember that almost all decisions can be corrected later.
  • Once you have chosen, stop looking at alternatives.

References

  1. Schwartz, B. et al. (2002). Maximizing versus satisficing: happiness is a matter of choice. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(5), 1178–1197.
  2. Iyengar, S. S., Wells, R. E. y Schwartz, B. (2006). Doing better but feeling worse: looking for the «best» job undermines satisfaction. Psychological Science, 17(2), 143–150.
  3. Gilbert, D. T. y Ebert, J. E. J. (2002). Decisions and revisions: the affective forecasting of changeable outcomes. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 82(4), 503–514.
  4. Weinshall-Margel, K. y Shapard, J. (2011). Overlooked factors in the analysis of parole decisions. PNAS, 108(42), E833.
  5. Hagger, M. S. et al. (2016). A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546–573.
